title: An experiment to investigate the nature of language ability

paragraphs.text: For some time scientists have debated the way in which humans acquire language. Underlying the debate is the question of whether humans learn language after birth, in much the same way as they learn other types of behaviour, or whether the human brain is pre-programmed. One line of investigation has involved the study of communication in other species, especially in primates like the chimpanzee. Since the 1980s, Sue Savage-Rumbaugh has been developing a new way of teaching language to chimps. Instead of training the chimps to learn symbols by rote, as other linguists had previously done, gradually building up a vocabulary one symbol at a time, Savage-Rumbaugh aimed to refer to a large vocabulary of symbols from the start, using the symbols in much the same way as language is used around human children. This represented a move away from an emphasis on language production, and towards an emphasis on comprehension. This new approach was used with bonobos – a species of chimp which is slightly smaller than the common chimp and more communicative through their facial expressions and gestures. Work with a bonobo called Matata began in 1981, but Matata did not come alone. Six months earlier, she had kidnapped a newborn infant and kept it as her own. This was Kanzi. While Savage-Rumbaugh and her colleagues were working with Matata, Kanzi was allowed to play freely. The researchers used a set of 256 geometrical shapes on a board. The instructors touched the shapes, which represented verbs and nouns, to create simple requests or commands. At the same time, they used ordinary spoken language.

Although Matata was clearly intelligent in many ways, she was a poor learner, and only used about six symbols. However, despite no attempt to teach Kanzi anything, he had picked up the symbols that Matata knew, as naturally as human children do. Once the researchers realised that, they made an even greater effort to place language learning in a context that was naturalistic. So a typical day for Kanzi and two other chimps was lace a field-based pre-school. Food could be found throughout a 50-acre forest. They had plenty of time off for social play with different companions, interesting places to visit, plus time for doing tests. At this time the chimps were asked to sit quietly and concentrate. The only instructions which the chimps’ carers were given were to communicate with them much as they would with very young children, except that they must accompany their speech with pointing to written symbols. The carers talked about things which were concrete and immediate, and used gestures and actions to make their meaning clear. There was no insistence that the chimps ‘talk’ (by using gestures and pointing to the written symbols), but the carers responded naturally if they did. In 1991, aged ten, Kanzi had a vocabulary of about 200 words. However, it was not the size of his vocabulary that was most impressive, but what the words seemed to mean to him. To test his ability, he was given verbal requests to do something, in sentence form, by someone out of his sight. The people in the same room as Kanzi wore earphones so they could not hear the instructions, and could not cue Kanzi, even unconsciously. None of the sentences was practised, and each one was different. Requests such as ‘Can you put the raisins in the bowl’, and ‘Can you give the cereal to Karen’ presented no problem for Kanzi. Nor did ‘Can you go to the colony room and get the telephone’. (The colony room was the chimps’ normal living area, and a few additional objects had been positioned there specifically for the purpose of the test.) A more demanding instruction was ‘Go to the colony room and get the orange’, when there was an orange in front of Kanzi. This caused him confusion about 90 percent of the time. But if asked to ‘Get the orange that’s in the colony room’ he did so without hesitation. This suggested that the sentences which were grammatically more complex were easier to understand than the simpler sentences. He also showed a grasp of grammatical rules concerning word order, for example that in two-word utterances such as ‘bring ball’, the action comes before the object. Significantly, he went from using a random order initially, to a clear, consistent order later.

Kanzi showed this level of understanding when he was nine years old, but not when he was younger than six. He was the first animal to demonstrate that observation is sufficient to acquire written sold spoken symbols. Other chimps (two bonobos and one common) have subsequently recognised symbols without training, so Kanzi’s ability is neither unique to him nor to his species.

Savage-Rumbaugh concluded that observational learning is a more powerful method of acquiring language than symbol training. She suggested that language training that is based on production is damaging. because it disrupts the ‘normal course’ of language acquisition. The best way for chimps to learn is through living in a structured environment, and by coming to understand what is said before choosing to use language.
